articles.author: Mayank Kumar
articles.description:
In short: a nested class is just a class written inside another class. It has no link to any outer object. Mark it inner and every instance keeps a hidden reference to the outer object. That lets it use the outer class's members, but it also keeps the outer object alive for as long as the inner one lives.
One keyword looks like a small change. In the bytecode, it adds a field to every object you create.
Have you ever added inner just to make a red error go away in Android Studio? It works, the code compiles, and you move on. But that keyword changes what your object holds in memory. In an Activity, that can be the difference between a clean screen and a leak.
This post covers what a nested class is, what inner adds, what the compiler generates for each, and when to use inner.
A nested clas…
articles.title: Inner vs Nested Class in Kotlin: What Is the Difference?

articles.author: Yunus Emre Güzel
articles.description:
You run your script. Python stops and prints this:
TypeError: 'int' object is not callable

It's a strange message. You probably never tried to "call" a number. Below you'll see what it means, the six situations that trigger it in real programs, and the fix for each one. I ran every example on Python 3.11, 3.12 and 3.14. All three print the same error.
Calling something means putting parentheses after it, like print(x), len(items) or score(3, 4). You can call functions, methods and classes. You can't call a number. So when Python hits something(...) and something holds an integer right now, it raises TypeError: 'int' object is not callable. The word in quotes is the type of the thing you tried to call. That's why you may also see 'str' object is not callable, 'list' object is not callable,…
articles.title: TypeError: ‘int’ Object Is Not Callable (Fix)
